name: SSRIs for BDD

card.summary: Antidepressants used for body dysmorphic disorder, a medical treatment rather than a looks tool.
card.note: Prescription drugs with a boxed warning for people under 25; used under medical supervision.

quick.overview:
SSRIs are antidepressants that are also used for obsessive-compulsive spectrum conditions, including body dysmorphic disorder. They are prescribed by clinicians as part of treatment for the disorder, often alongside therapy.

They are not appearance-enhancement products and are discussed here only in their role in BDD care.
quick.mechanism: They block reuptake of serotonin, raising its availability between nerve cells; with continued use the brain adapts in ways that are thought to relate to their effects.
quick.risks: Common class effects include sexual side effects and emotional blunting; stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and an FDA boxed warning advises monitoring people under 25 for suicidal thoughts. They are prescription-only.

lead: SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) are antidepressants prescribed for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition in which a person is preoccupied with perceived flaws in their appearance. They are used to reduce the obsessive preoccupation, mirror checking and distress, so that people see and feel about their own appearance more accurately and can function and socialise normally.[2][4]

The NHS describes treatment as depending on severity: cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for mild BDD, CBT or an SSRI for moderate, and CBT combined with an SSRI for severe cases or when other treatments have not worked; fluoxetine is the most commonly used SSRI.[4] Wikipedia describes SSRIs and CBT as effective treatments, with SSRIs easing obsessive-compulsive and delusional features.[2]

This matters for appearance communities because many people with BDD seek cosmetic or dermatological procedures, which Wikipedia reports typically do not resolve their distress, and it recommends surgeons and psychiatrists screen for BDD together.[2] SSRIs are prescription medicines used under medical supervision; this article gives general information only.

chain: SSRI raises serotonin availability and eases obsessive preoccupation
Less fixation on perceived flaws, mirror checking and distress
More accurate self-view and less pursuit of procedures aimed at the perceived flaw
angle.text: SSRIs do not change how someone looks; they are used to reduce the obsessive focus and distress in BDD, which can change how a person sees their appearance and how they live with it. Clinicians commonly combine them with CBT.

paras: BDD is classified in the obsessive-compulsive spectrum in the DSM-5, and SSRIs are used in it as they are in obsessive-compulsive disorder.[2][1] The NHS says SSRIs can take up to 12 weeks to work and are usually continued for several months, with gradual dose reduction when stopping.[4]

Wikipedia's BDD article describes CBT as helping patients recognise faulty thought patterns, and cites a treatment manual by Sabine Wilhelm and colleagues built on psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual prevention, and mindfulness and perceptual retraining.[2] In OCD, Wikipedia reports that SSRIs are first-line in some national guidelines, and that in children and adolescents combining them with exposure therapy is probably more effective than an SSRI alone.[1]

Wikipedia reports that many people with BDD seek dermatological treatment or cosmetic surgery, which often fails to relieve symptoms because the distress is not grounded in the actual appearance. It cites a meta-analysis estimating about 24% of plastic surgery patients, 18% of psychiatric patients and 16% of dermatology patients had BDD, while giving a general-population figure that varies between 2-3% and about 17% in different parts of the article.[2]

Reported effects of the SSRI class include sexual dysfunction, emotional blunting, bleeding risk, akathisia and, rarely, serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs. Stopping abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms.[1] The FDA's boxed warning advises close monitoring of people under 25 for increased suicidal thoughts and behavior, concentrated in the first one to two months of treatment, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1] The NHS likewise says doctors monitor closely early on, especially in children, adults under 30 and people with a history of suicidal behaviour.[4]

A registered phase 4 trial, 'CBT as an Adjunct to SRIs in the Treatment of BDD', began in 2008 and was terminated after enrolling 17 people.[3] Larger trial results on SSRIs for BDD were not located here.

timeline.event: Phase 4 trial of CBT added to SRIs in BDD registered; later terminated.[3]
